utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good morning to everyone. Mr. Registrar, would you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. This is case number IT-00-39-T, the Prosecutor versus Momcilo Krajisnik.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Registrar. Mr. Stewart before I invite to you continue the examination-in-chief, I'd like to remind you, Mr. Krajisnik, that you are still bound by the solemn declaration you've given at the beginning of your testimony.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Stewart, you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. May I mention one practical thing to do with team membership, Your Honour, we have the pleasure of introducing a temporary new member of the team --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: She's gone already.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Well, she's temporarily gone. And she hasn't walked out in disgust yet. But, Your Honour, we did wish Your Honours to know that the reason you're not seeing Mr. Karganovic in court anymore is because he has left the team. He left the team with effect from the end of April. He was our case manager, Your Honour. But, Your Honour, I must say I am aware that sometimes very inaccurate information floats around the place about the reasons for team arrivals, departures and so on, so I just want to make it publicly clear that Mr. Karganovic has left because we simply do not have the money to pay him anymore, and it's as simple as that. And I would just like to express publicly my thanks to Mr. Karganovic for his loyalty to the Defence team over that period. And just for Your Honours to know that we -- Ms. Pitcher is taking over the role of -- Kelly Pitcher, our case manager. But that's the reason, it's the only reason, Your Honour. That's what has happened.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you very much. Although no rumours yet arrived. So no wrong information was there. It's always good to have the right information directly.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: I like to head them off in advance, Your Honour, sometimes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honours, Mr. Krajisnik, we were looking at and we were getting towards the end of the minutes of the Fourth Session of the Assembly of the Serb People of Bosnia-Herzegovina. We were at page 40 of the English. It was -- sorry, Mr. Krajisnik, it's where we had got to yesterday. It was in the speech of Mr. Karadzic, Dr. Karadzic. Point 22 was some pages before. It's point 22 in the margin. We had been looking at quite a long speech. There is a decision with 19 numbered items and then a page or two on, Dr. Karadzic's speech, quite a long speech. And then there is a reference to passage the -- I've got to find it for you, Mr. Krajisnik. It's --

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think it's number 16, if I'm not mistaken -- no, sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: We are going to give you the page number, Mr. Krajisnik, as soon as Mr. --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If Mr. Krajisnik has found number 16, there seems to be no problem but ...

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: It's not number 16 we are looking for ultimately, Your Honour. My apologies, Your Honour. It's my fault. I didn't have the B/C/S cross-reference.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's probably 77, my page number, 5138 being the last numbers. SA025138.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That's at least the beginning of a speech of Mr. --

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: It's in the middle of page 82. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Middle of page 82, Mr. Krajisnik, a paragraph beginning: "We, therefore, suggest the establishment of three entities." Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes, I see that.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Middle of page 40 in the English. "We, therefore, suggest the establishment of three entities in BiH which would not threaten or confront each other. On the contrary, they should at most complement each other or at least be neutral and impartial towards each other so that common institutions could be formed at the level of BiH, that is, the existing republic of BiH. "How could it become a link in those -- in these circumstances? It could become a link if the Serbian Bosnia and Herzegovina could exercise its right to remain within Yugoslavia and form some common institutions with Yugoslavia. Muslim Bosnia and Herzegovina could decide whether it wanted to have any links with Yugoslavia or only confederal links with the Serbian Bosnia and Herzegovina. The Croatian Bosnia and Herzegovina could decide whether or not it wanted any links with Croatia, e.g. federal, but at the same time it should have some links with Bosnia-Herzegovina. Although this proposal looks complicated and unique, and indeed it is complicated and unique, as is BiH itself, we think that it can be realised. It is better than civil war. As rational beings, we know what civil war means; the experience of Croatia tells us exactly what civil war has done to us." Mr. Krajisnik, does it follow from what were you saying yesterday that this particular idea that Dr. Karadzic was outlining here was coming as something new to at least a significant number of the deputies present?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. You're right. And that will be evident from the discussion that followed. There is one contribution in particular from which you will see the level of surprise on the part of some individuals.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Well, so we can make sure we come to it at the right time, you have a particular name of a particular deputy in mind, Mr. Krajisnik, there, do you?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Specifically, at this session, Mrs. Plavsic spoke, and you can see from her contribution that she doesn't understand how come we are now linking up into a confederation with Muslims and on the other hand we want Yugoslavia, but Karadzic cut that short, saying that --

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: I'll cut you short, if I may, on that without any impoliteness. I just want you to be sure, we are going to come to Mrs. Plavsic's contribution so we can take that in its order. Thank you. The -- but you yourself had had some discussion with Dr. Karadzic, didn't come as a surprise to you, did it, what Dr. Karadzic was saying?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I said yesterday that there was a turnabout in the vision of things that I had learned about from Mr. Karadzic and Mr. Milosevic. I think Mr. Koljevic attended that meeting but I don't know who else. I know Mrs. Plavsic wasn't there. I'm talking now about the negotiators, out of that circle.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: And then Dr. Karadzic goes on in the same passage: "Apart from causing the deaths of several hundred thousand people and complete destruction of several hundred towns, a civil war in Bosnia and Herzegovina would also result in massive and rapid population movements. In other words, it would lead to population homogenisation. What would be the end result of it all? The end result would be the situation as it is today: Separate Serbian, Croatian and Muslim areas left impoverished by several hundred towns and several hundred thousand people." First of all, Mr. Krajisnik, can you explain when Dr. Karadzic was saying "the end result would be the situation as it is today," it's very clear he doesn't mean that literally. What did you understand him to be saying?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Specifically concerning this passage, I could define it as follows: What Mr. Karadzic is saying is that his proposal is better than war, because the war would have the same consequences, it would leave us in the same place, with many more adverse consequences, and it makes it incumbent upon us to continue negotiating, to find a solution, because we have to find a political solution between the warring parties. A solution has to be politically verified. That was the main objective of our policy that we were trying to present to the MPs.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Do you agree, just as a starting point, that what Dr. Karadzic is saying is, in that last sentence, today we got separate Serbian, Croatian and Muslim areas. If we have a war, we'll still have that but we will have lost several hundred towns and several hundred thousand people, that that's a summary of what he's saying? Do you agree? You're nodding, Mr. Krajisnik. The tape won't pick up a nod.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. You're right. I didn't look at the text, but I see that he actually says we already have some -- already established regions, Croat, Serb and Muslims, and after a war we would have the same thing, only compounded by many other adverse consequences. You're completely right.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Now, how -- how complete did you regard the degree of separation among Serbian and Croatian and Muslim areas as being at this time, December 1991?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, when a state is being broken up, the degree of separation is much greater, and to the misfortune of that one entity, the degree of separation between regions was rather high. As for the Muslim and Croat majority, they had power on the municipal level in their respective regions. So communities, which had a relative majority, had also power in their respective municipalities. I'm now talking about the Muslim and Croat areas.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: When Dr. Karadzic referred there to a civil war resulting in massive and rapid population movements, first of all, did you share his view that that would be the result of civil war?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: You can study war from books as much as you like, but you never learn about it so well as you do from direct participants, people who survived a war, and we heard from our parents about the Second World War, about the experience of those who were a minority in one area and had to leave their homes and were expelled and had to move. So we knew that if a war should break out, there would be population movements and nobody would be happy. It was not about what you call ethnic cleansing. It's a phenomenon that comes inevitably with a war. In every war, inevitably a certain percentage of the population flees their homes. That's some sort of family memory that every -- every family had from the Second World War. However, with regard to the Muslim people, there is a term "mujahir" [phoen]. That means refugees. And after the Second World War, there was talk about how many people had fled, how many ended up as refugees. So we had both practical and theoretical knowledge and experience about it, and I am making a distinction now between "mujahir," refugee, and "mujahedin." It's not the same thing.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Mr. Krajisnik, can we get this clear? You used the phrase "ethnic cleansing" in that last answer. You said this was not about what you or what one calls ethnic cleansing. It's not a technical, legal term, ethnic cleansing. What do you understand by the term "ethnic cleansing"?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, having spent as long as I have here in prison, I have learned about the term of ethnic cleansing, and naturally, during the war, I had heard that term as well. Ethnic cleansing means forcing people, against their will, people belonging to a certain ethnic community, to move, expelling them from their homes. That term implies that something is done by force, applying various instruments. For a more elaborate explanation, you should ask a lawyer, but to me it means driving out a certain group, a certain minority, belonging to a different ethnicity by force, by coercion, making them move to a different territory. That's how I understood the term "ethnic cleansing," as I heard it here, and also during the war. That means forcing an ethnic group to move.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Mr. Krajisnik, when Dr. Karadzic was talking there about civil war resulting in massive and rapid population movements, did you understand him to be including in what he was saying about that result ethnic cleansing as one of the causes of such movements?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: This was in December 1991, and this is the presentation of Mr. Karadzic about the move of the population who were fleeing war. That term "ethnic cleansing" was not used in the Second World War, whereas he was talking about the Second World War and what happened then. People were moving, trying to escape from the war. He was only talking about population movements that would necessarily come if war broke out. People moving out of fear, looking for safety. There was no mention of driving people or expelling people or applying force. All the negotiations that took place before the war concentrated exclusively on finding a peaceful solution that implied that everybody would stay where they were.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: So, Mr. Krajisnik, let's get some, if you like, ground rules clear. It appears from the evidence that we've heard in this case that the phrase "ethnic cleansing," in unhappily very common use now, was probably coined during this particular conflict, so that in December 1991 it doesn't appear to have been a term in common usage. That seems to be what we get from the evidence. Whether or not that's 100 per cent right perhaps doesn't matter. If I am now asking you at any time about ethnic cleansing, in my questions to you, Mr. Krajisnik, I am, for the moment, adopting your definition as you gave it just now. So if I'm asking you a question which includes that phrase, that's the concept I'm asking you about. We can all argue until the end of time about ethnic cleansing at some future point, but that's -- is that clear what I'm -- what I'm doing and how I'm using the phrase then in questions to you?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Stewart, if you would use that I'd like to seek one clarification in order to better understand the testimony. Mr. Krajisnik, you used the word "by force," you used the word "coercion." Would that include making life so miserable by whatever means that people hardly had any other choice than to leave, that is, deprive them from privileges -- well, you have heard during the course of the case quite a lot of examples. Would that be included in the words "force" or "coercion" you used, or would you limit that exclusively to taking people -- taking them away, forcing them to -- physically forcing them to leave the area? Since Mr. Stewart is going to use your definition as the starting point of his questions, I'd like to have clarity on that point.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It is certain that I should have provided a broader explanation. As to your question, Your Honour, if the majority deliberately created insufferable conditions that make a person hardly wait to leave, of course, that constitutes ethnic cleansing. But in a war, the distinction between something that is done deliberately and something that is simply brought on by the war itself, as a result of the war, is very difficult to make. When I said forcing somebody to leave, I didn't mean necessarily rounding up people. If somebody in power intimidated the other side, the other group, of course, those people will leave. But if a person or a group left because they were afraid of what might happen and then after the war they come back and say, "Somebody drove me out actually, it's not that I left out of fear," that is quite different. So I would answer your question like this: If somebody deliberately created difficult conditions of life for a group or for an individual, then that comes very close to ethnic cleansing. However, conditions in certain areas were very hard and still people stayed on. And then the Dayton Accords came and some people started claiming being victims of ethnic cleansing in retrospect. You have the problem of the freedom of movement. Everybody should be able to go wherever they like. And two different rights are in conflict. If you enable somebody to leave, he will say he was ethnically cleansed. If you don't allow him to leave, then he is an ethnic hostage. So every municipality, every town, every particular case, should be analysed separately to see how much of each of these two elements is present in the movements of population. Do you know how many people from Sarajevo left before the war even broke out? Planeloads of people. People left for different reasons. And I wouldn't like for a minute -- I myself am a refugee. I would never, ever absolve somebody who made life so difficult for others that those others had to leave. Leaving your home is very difficult. You never forget your home. But you have very difficult cases. Different cases contain elements so similar that it's very difficult to make a distinction. Of course, I can't say that there was no coercion and no forcible moves of population. Of course that happened. But to summarise, if somebody deliberately creates insufferable conditions, that is close to ethnic cleansing. It's not quite the same as ethnic cleansing. Conditions of life were very difficult and still people stayed on; whereas in other areas, conditions were less hard and still people left. That is quite honestly how I see this question. And I lived there. I know. I know at least about the community where I lived and that I'm familiar with.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I do understand that you would like to make a difference between those anticipating on what might happen and out of fear of what would happen and those who were taken by the circumstances, sometimes perhaps created deliberately and sometimes just being consequences of a war situation. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Please, Your Honour, just one more thing. I'll be very sincere. Look at how hard the conditions were in Zenica, Tuzla, Sarajevo, for everybody but people stayed; whereas there is another town where the situation was quite liveable, so to speak, and people of all ethnic communities left. And I'm absolutely sincere in saying that people left for all sorts of reasons, and I can enumerate them. People -- men sometimes left leaving their women and children behind out of fear, because they were afraid of the war, and then blamed somebody else. I'm sorry for taking so much time. I wanted to be quite clear.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Your answer is perfectly clear. It's also clear how you explained that it's sometimes difficult to make a distinction, but that it should be made. Please proceed, Mr. Stewart.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Mr. Krajisnik, when Dr. Karadzic was referring there to civil war resulting in massive and rapid population movements, did you understand him to be saying that there would be driving out of members of any ethnic group by other ethnic groups?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Absolutely not. And I can give you an example that will make it quite clear. Something that happened later, if you're interested.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Well, perhaps you could just very briefly say what the example is, Mr. Krajisnik, and then we might consider whether to come to it in due course or to deal with it now. Could you just indicate what it is that you're talking about?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think Jews left Sarajevo, not Muslims, not Croats and not Serbs. He meant that the war inevitably makes some people leave. Let us leave aside all the other negative things. People go somewhere else where they will fare better but the Jews left for Israel. Population movements sometimes happen without any action being taken. That's what Mr. Karadzic meant. I never heard him say otherwise.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: When he said there that -- he said: "In other words, it would lead to population homogenisation." Now, the individual words are fairly clear in their meaning, Mr. Krajisnik, but in saying that it would lead to population homogenisation, what did you understand him to mean as that result of population homogenisation?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember how I understood it then, but I can explain how I understand it now. Population homogenisation implies that people who are a minority in one place tended to go to another place where their ethnic community was in majority. That's one. Second, people who were pacifists, who did not have particular feelings of ethnic affiliation tended to side with their ethnic communities because they were branded by the other side as Serbs, Croats, whatever, and they did not feel that they were on an equal footing. Of course, there were other ethnic groups apart from these three main ethnic communities, but we are mainly talking about Serbs, Croats and Muslims. So the homogenisation was two-pronged.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Leaving aside the prospect that it might result from a civil war, was population homogenisation something which you regarded as a positive result?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no. It wasn't good. When homogenisation of the population is carried out -- it's not natural. I mean in war. It's not natural because the war made people side with their ethnic communities in areas where they are a majority, and the war makes them move. The situation itself makes people move to places where their community is in the majority. It's a consequence of the war. And Dr. Karadzic is talking about the possible consequences of war. And we discussed it yesterday. We were saying that at that time we discussed a new concept, saying that, let's not go to war, let's try to avoid war, let's try to find a different solution.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: It's my fault. I'm not making myself sufficiently clear. Perhaps it's because war is rather a large thing to put on one side. I'll -- so I'll make it clearer. Do you agree, the extreme form of population homogenisation is where you have some areas containing, let's say, only Serbs and other areas containing only Muslims and other areas containing only Croats. That's the absolute extreme of population homogenisation, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, you're completely right. And that's the kind of homogenisation that I called negative. That's one of the consequences of war. That's what we would have if war broke out.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Krajisnik, as Dr. Karadzic himself, it's an obvious point, says, one of the terrible consequences of war is that a very large number of people are likely to be killed. That's what he's saying. That's obvious, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I mean -- well, Mr. Karadzic said a logical thing. People get killed in a war. In every war that took place in our part of the world, there were many, many victims, like in other states probably. Again I'm relying on experience. Most casualties come in a civil war. I'm talking about the civil war between the three peoples within that one whole.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Mr. Krajisnik, I didn't want to dwell in a sense on that serious but obvious point. I want to make it clear that I'm asking you about a situation in which there was no war. Population homogenisation in the context of there being no war. Was it SDS policy at this time that even if there was not a war, you wanted to move towards a high degree of population homogenisation in Bosnia and Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's always a problem to interpret a question. I don't know how I could explain this in a more persuasive fashion. Not at a single point in time did we want to have pure territories and to have some kind of homogenisation of Serbs in one territory. I'm talking about a peaceful settlement to the crisis in Bosnia-Herzegovina. Where one particular ethnic community is a majority, or the second one, or the third one, that is the kind of entities that would exist. Now, if we were to advocate something in an artificial manner, let me be quite honest about this. The setting up of two ethnic communities or, rather, parties, national parties, and then the third party, the Serb Democratic Party, when that happened, it's amazing to what extent people identified with these parties. Before that, in the elections they would have voted for other parties that were not national parties. However, as the crisis was aggravated, people identified to a larger extent with the national parties. That is what a crisis is. However, we did not want to have this kind of homogenisation to say that we should have 80 per cent or 90 per cent Serbs, and in another area there should be Muslims or Croats, because the point was to look at the percentages of the population in order to see what these territorial units would be. But this homogenisation would not be carried out on political grounds or anything. It's my understanding that he was talking about a war, what a war would bring about, population movements and things like that. He was not talking about peace and homogenisation. He was talking about the consequences of a war and homogenisation. So my answer to your question is as follows: We did not advocate homogenisation because automatically in a peaceful way -- well, it's not that we had a plan of this kind, because that would have left to a second homogenisation and a third homogenisation. You would be living in peace and, on the other hand, you would not be living in peace. It is indispensable to have cooperation and mingling. But it is important for everyone to be master in one's own territory, in the majority of one's own territories.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Would, as you saw it at the time, Mr. Krajisnik, would the establishment of three entities in Bosnia and Herzegovina by peaceful means involve significant population movements?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm convinced that that would not have happened. Perhaps at first some people would have left but people would have gone back. Everybody likes to live where they live. I like my own "zabrdje." Even if they were to give Paris or Madrid to me on a platter, I would prefer it. Everybody likes the place there are they come from. So perhaps there would be these individual cases, but when there is peace and when there are no boundaries, when you can just cross them, then, yes, thank you -- thank you, Mr. President. Perhaps it's a question of temperament. I'm speaking very loud and very fast. A war is a different situation. Well, we had municipalities, you see. In one municipality there would be one tax, and in another municipality there would be another tax, so it's not all the same to you but then, on the other hand, you stay where -- in the place where you're from. I'm convinced that it is a great, great pity that we did not continue along the charted course, if I can put it that way, and why we did not find a political solution and why Bosnia was not recognised that way. That would have been a happy republic, if I can put it that way, and an internationally recognised entity. Now I don't want to be partial and to say everybody is to blame. After all, history will be the judge of that. I'm sorry, and I apologise to the interpreters as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Can we go on, while inviting Your Honours not to ignore the next few paragraphs because they are part of a quite important speech. But if we go on a few paragraphs to middle of page 41 of the English, and can you pick up a very short paragraph, one line probably, or two lines, Mr. Krajisnik, that says: "Sovereignty primarily means power, the ultimate power over oneself." It will be a page or so on from where we have just been.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Page 84, the semi-last paragraph.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: "Sovereignty primarily means power." But I'm going to the next paragraph. "Therefore, we could agree on the possibility of the Serbian, Croatian and Muslim peoples exercising sovereign power over each other; a possibility which would involve the establishment of a political union of Bosnia and Herzegovina; a union which could one day provide a genuine 'link' which could reconnect people, should the goodwill for such reconnection exist after all this. But at this point in time, given the great deal of suspicion among people and the danger of civil war and destruction, our proposal that I explained earlier is such and I urge you to examine and discuss it today. What I mean is that you suggest specific proposals for specific cities, and in particular, for Sarajevo, which could have an extraterritorial status and where Serbs, Croats and Muslims could each organise their own administration." Is it a -- is it a correct understanding of what Dr. Karadzic is saying that he was throwing the matter open to suggestions and inviting proposals from deputies in relation to particular places in Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, there is a sentence here that is a bit perplexing for those who read this for the first time. He's saying that Croats and Muslims could perhaps create a sovereign republic of their own and that that would be a link with our republic, if there is a will, along those lines. At this moment there is not enough confidence, et cetera, et cetera. One has to understand that here Mr. Karadzic is trying in a soft way to prepare the deputies and the others for the turnaround which had not been disclosed yet. He's introducing different elements which are a bit illogical as well. Now, what you were saying or, rather, what you were asking, that's the point. The point is that they should present different proposals and he gave one for Sarajevo. I have a newspaper article here a statement made by Mr. Karadzic about Sarajevo after the Cutileiro negotiations when he said exactly what our position was. And that was our position throughout. Please, if you want, you will see that it's not a division. It's precisely in this way, to have an extraterritorial part to create a municipality, to have some council and so on and so forth. No one ever mentioned any walls. And then you have Sarajevo and then perhaps Banja Luka. I mean I'm just inventing names of towns now, but I was just trying to say let's try to have as many proposals as possible so that we would be prepared to negotiate with the other two ethnic communities or whoever we may be talking to. Or what is it that we want to achieve? We as the Serb side, what is our position? What do we want to achieve?

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Did the -- this Sarajevo proposal here, was that something which came from you or to which you had made a contribution in discussion before this meeting?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I was one of the few Sarajevo-born people in the entire political establishment. Out of the leading people, nobody was born in Sarajevo. I loved Sarajevo very much and, of course, I loved the interests of the Serb people because this was the second-ranking Serb town. You will see the map that we proposed to Mr. Cutileiro. We said, "Look, let this be under the UN, Sarajevo. And let us try to find a specific solution so that within Bosnia-Herzegovina, this should be a solution that would be a link so that these two entities, or three entities, I beg your pardon, would be linked up. The joint institutions would be there and everything else." I always expressed a keen interest in order to make an effort to find a special solution for Sarajevo. Now did I say this to Mr. Karadzic? He shared my views but I guess this is his proposal. I don't think that I suggested anything to him before this, but later on I took active part in possible solutions for Sarajevo. Today, regrettably, Sarajevo is divided, without the Serbs. We could have had a city that had not been divided had there been a bit more wisdom but ...

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Could we move on, please, Mr. Krajisnik, from Dr. Karadzic's speech, then? The next speaker is Mr. Nedic and then Mr. Vojnovic, and then Mr. Koljevic, and then we come in a few pages to Dr. Kalinic. That's page 45 of the English.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I think --

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: 93 of your version, Mr. Krajisnik. Dr. Karadzic --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: There are a few other speakers as well.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Yes, there are a whole lot of speakers, Mr. Cizmovic, Mr. Pejovic and then to Dr. Kalinic. It was just really to find him, Your Honour. I won't read everything of Dr. Kalinic here. The third or fourth paragraph in what he says, he says: "I think that our absolute minimum at the moment" -- do you see that?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Last two lines of the page.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: In the English, Your Honour. I don't know what it is in --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No, I said last to lines in the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: It is by coincidence the last two lines in both, Your Honour. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: "I think that out of absolute minimum..."

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Yes, yes. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: "... absolute minimum at the moment, which we as representatives of the Serbian people, regardless of our party affiliation, can agree upon is the proposal for the establishment of the three national communities in the territory of today's Bosnia and Herzegovina. "Of course, if our proposal is rejected in the course of the ongoing negotiations, and according to my understanding of the situation there are going to be limited to 14 January 2002, ladies and gentlemen who are negotiating with us should be in no doubt about our response. We have the solution that we presented today, which is the establishment of independent Serbian political institutions in the territories where they make the majority of the population." Mr. Krajisnik, was Dr. Kalinic saying that he would, however reluctantly, accept independence of Bosnia and Herzegovina on the footing that there would be the establishment of three national communities in the territory of Bosnia and Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That's what Mr. Kalinic said, as president of the club of the reformist forces in the parliament of Bosnia-Herzegovina, which then acceded to the Serb Assembly.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: About three paragraphs further on, or four paragraphs further on, he starts: "Let me say this quite clearly." Do you see that? You can skip over three paragraphs. Then he says: "Let me say this quite clearly."

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: "And I hope you share my views on this matter," he continues, "that no one has the right to deny the Muslim people, who have their tradition, history and natural right to be sovereign, to establish their own nation state, but only on the territories, and here I shall use Mr. Izetbegovic's expression, which they make viable and prosperous in the long run." Mr. Krajisnik, wherever originally that phrase came from, what did you or do you understand by that reference to "their own nation state, [being] only on territories ... which they make viable and prosperous in the long run"?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the talks with the three ethnic communities, what was discussed was how a sovereign Bosnia would be introduced in the territories where the Serbs are a majority and where they control power. I was not present at this discussion that I'm going to refer to now, but I heard about it from Mr. Karadzic and Mr. Koljevic. At that time the Muslim side said we are going to proclaim a sovereign Bosnia in the territories where we can control them prosperously. That is where Bosnia is going to be and that is where we are going to be in power. They meant the places where they were actually in power, where they were in government. That's what came from the Muslim side and that's what I heard from Mr. Karadzic and Mr. Koljevic, that either Mr. Izetbegovic said or Mr. Rasim Kadic. Please don't take my word for it now. But here, Mr. Kalinic is saying that it was Mr. Izetbegovic who said that, but the meaning is the one that I refer to just now. That's what it relates to.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Did you understand there to be a significant difference between what the Muslims were saying, as you've just reported it in that answer, in relation to what might become their sovereign territory, and what the Bosnian Serbs were saying in relation to what might become their sovereign territory?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: When you look at the map of Bosnia-Herzegovina, if you're a Serb, everything is blue to you. If you're a Muslim, everything is green to you. If you're a Croat, everything is yellow to you. It depends on the glasses that you're wearing. We don't know what they think. We know what the Serb side thinks. That is why it was indispensable for the three sides to reach agreement. You cannot know with what kind of glasses a Muslim is looking at this map. They see everything green. When I say "green," I mean the colour on the map that denotes where the Muslims are a majority; and yellow where the Croats are a majority; and blue where the Serbs are a majority. So what you said, regardless of what people thought, and people probably thought along different lines, it was necessary to sit down and reach an agreement in order for it to be said exactly what should be done. Mr. Cutileiro gave a solution for that, the census of '71, '81, '91, who had a majority where, so that there could be this exchange of territories. That was almost taken care of. That was almost done. It wouldn't depend on what kind of glasses we were wearing. What I'm talking about glasses, I'm speaking in a figurative manner. I, as a Serb, wear glasses through which I see Serb colours and a Serb majority everywhere and so on and so forth.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Mr. Krajisnik, could you go on to page 97 in your version? And this is page 47 in the English, Your Honours. There is a short contribution by you: "Chairman: "Thank you very much. Ladies and gentlemen, dear guests, if you will allow me I shall make a little comment before we start voting on the proposal that has been put forward. Please remember when we say something -- that when we say something about decisions we are taking here today we are sending a message not only to the Serbian people but to all nations ... of Bosnia and Herzegovina." And then Mrs. Plavsic, this may or may not be what you were referring to earlier, but Mrs. Plavsic begins: "I should say something because I do not quite understand it. Some things are not quite clear to me and perhaps they should be, since I was authorised by this Assembly to take part in these negotiations, the negotiations with the two parties mentioned earlier. "By the way, I did not take part in these negotiations but this is not the reason why I wanted to address you. The reason why I wanted to address you is this idea of confederation. I am not at all clear about what it means." First of all, Mr. Krajisnik, why did Mrs. Plavsic not take part in the negotiations?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Assembly authorised seven persons, and she was one of the seven. You find the answer why she didn't participate just down below, as explained by Mr. Karadzic. Other sides wanted to have direct, bilateral talks. Karadzic, Izetbegovic; Karadzic, Kljuic, et cetera. So Karadzic, in order not to be alone, expanded the delegation. I was a member of the delegation of Bosnia-Herzegovina talking to other republics, so we held the primary role in this group. Mrs. Plavsic is expressing here her dissatisfaction over why she wasn't involved, and Mr. Buha and Mr. Koljevic were also negotiators. I looked at this just last night so I remember it quite well.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Mr. Krajisnik, we can see a little bit later on, it's in the middle of page 48 of the English, I won't trouble you with the detailed reference, but we can see that Dr. Karadzic says: "We didn't want to bother Mrs. Plavsic with procedural matters." But sometimes people say things, Mr. Krajisnik. Was Mrs. Plavsic excluded from the negotiating team because Dr. Karadzic didn't want her on the negotiating team?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. If I had to make a guess, I would say that it's rather the MPs who didn't want her on the negotiating team and the other side that didn't want her there, because Mrs. Plavsic had already displayed her radicalism on the Presidency and that was witnessed by Mr. Kljuic and Mr. Izetbegovic, so they preferred to talk to Mr. Karadzic and myself. Mr. Karadzic always believed actually that Mrs. Plavsic was the best defender of Serb interests, and he even later named her as his successor. But on this occasion she was really excluded from the negotiations, for several reasons. She wasn't really cut out to make compromises. She was in favour of cut-and-dried solutions, like a Serb state. But to be quite precise, I don't know which of the reasons, which of the various reasons, prevailed here.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, Mr. Sladojevic assures me that on page 25, lines 3 and 4 of the transcript, where it said "that was witnessed by Mr. Kljuic and Mr. Izetbegovic, so they preferred to talk to Mr. Karadzic and myself," that in fact the Serbian translated ought to be "Mr. Karadzic and us."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You could verify the matter with the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Mr. Krajisnik, you gave an answer, you said, the whole sentence was -- I'd asked you whether it was that Dr. Karadzic didn't want Mrs. Plavsic on the negotiating team. You said if you had a make a guess you would say it's rather the MPs who didn't want her on the negotiating team and the other side that didn't want her there, because Mrs. Plavsic had already displayed her radicalism on the Presidency and that was witnessed by Mr. Kljuic and Mr. Izetbegovic, so they preferred to talk to, and then, well, you've heard the question is whether you then said preferred to talk to Mr. Karadzic and myself, you, Mr. Krajisnik, or Mr. Karadzic and us. Do you remember, Mr. Krajisnik, what you said?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yesterday I said Mr. Sladojevic is right and he's right again. "With us." I can add to it later. I meant Mr. Koljevic and myself, for other reasons which have nothing to do with your question for the moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: It was Mr. Karadzic, Mr. Koljevic and yourself?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: You were the negotiating team for all practical purposes, weren't you?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, that was the time when this pre-war Bosnia-Herzegovina still existed. Mr. Koljevic and I held official posts. We were in office and Mr. Karadzic was party leader. So that's the team that was formed after the abortive delegations for talks among republics, republic to republic. Mr. Koljevic replaced Mr. -- Mrs. Plavsic as head of our delegation.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Now, you've previously been asked by one of Their Honours, Mr. Krajisnik, when you used the term "radical" or "radicalism," you've been asked a more specific question. You said that -- so similarly, when you said that Mrs. Plavsic had already displayed her radicalism, what are the essential characteristics of that radicalism that she had displayed?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I'm wrong like many other people when I call this radicalism. I'll explain what I meant. In negotiations, you have to bear in mind that there is the other side, too, that has its own interests and you should strive for a compromise. You should not be narrow-minded. Sometimes you're perhaps asking for more in order to be able to achieve an optimum. If you just stay put, without moving anywhere, and if you state that publicly, of course, you're irritating the other side. They feel unpleasant, and they say, I cannot reach any kind of agreement with you. Through negotiations, you often present your views. The other side understands you. As soon as they understand you, they resist what you want less. When I'm talking about Mrs. Plavsic, Mrs. Plavsic is now -- well, perhaps I'm not going to be partial -- impartial at other moments, but I'll try to be as impartial as possible now but I have reason to be angry with her. At that time, Mrs. Plavsic, as a woman, had a problem with all those men around her. All the others on the Presidency were men. So as a woman, she fought just in case. As best she could, and knew how to, she defended Serb interests in that Presidency but she didn't have these diplomatic skills to present this properly. She would simply come out with what she thought so she would come out in an undiplomatic way believing that she would help the Serb people in that way. However, that would lead us further away from an agreement. We started some discussions a hundred times from one position, and then we would come to a completely different position and then we would say well this is an optimal solution, then we would accept it. That's what I meant when I said "radicalism," although that word radicalism is not right. It's lack of diplomacy, lack of willingness to reach a compromise or something like that. But believe me, whenever Mrs. Plavsic advocated something, she was right almost always. However, it's not sufficient to be right if you're negotiating. You have to be a bit more flexible in order to somehow exercise that right of yours. Now, I'm talking about someone for whom I don't have much sympathy but this is the truth.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Mrs. Plavsic continued: "Why should we, as a unit within this imagined 'confederation,' enter in any kind of relationship with the Muslim and Croatian national communities. We can enter into a relationship with these two communities only as a unit within Yugoslavia so that Yugoslavia defines its relations with them. Only under this condition can we enter into any sort of relationship with them." Mr. Krajisnik, that was taken and understood, was it, as Mrs. Plavsic rejecting the idea which was being floated by Dr. Karadzic for three separate entities as a negotiated solution?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. She wanted a Serb state, to unite with Serbia, with Yugoslavia, and then that Yugoslavia would be linked up to this remainder of Bosnia. That's clear. You see that there was applause here. Many MPs wanted that, that's absolutely the case, but that was not realistic, and that is why Mr. Karadzic later tried to explain this. You can wish to have New York, but it's not realistic. So that's why he tried to explain this here now. She didn't want a solution that was realistic. She went for a wishful thinking in terms of what she thought was best. But let me say under quotation marks, she was right, because only yesterday, so to speak, the Muslim and the Croat said that they didn't want to compromise, that they wanted independence of Bosnia-Herzegovina. If that's what you want, then of course her reaction is, well, we don't want to be with you if you don't want to be with us. However, that was not realistic. I've already said that and that's why Karadzic was now slowly preparing, in the talks, the existence of three constituent units and the recognition of Bosnia-Herzegovina as an independent internationally recognised state. There is a telephone conversation here, we had it, where Karadzic and I were talking about this and analysing this and saying, whatever happened to Biljana? Actually, she was not "au courant," so that's why she reacted in this uncontrolled way.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Then the next paragraph of what Dr. Plavsic says is: "Why should we, the Serbs, the Republic of Serbian Bosnia and Herzegovina enter into any kind of relationship with say, the Republic of Muslim Bosnia and Herzegovina. There is going to be no relationship!" Did you -- for practical purposes, Mr. Krajisnik, did you know that Mrs. Plavsic was going to be opposed to what Dr. Karadzic was suggesting?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was surprised. I thought that Mr. Karadzic had talked to her. I don't know how. I was surprised, because it does carry weight when a member of the Presidency is saying something that is opposite to what many MPs felt. That was a surprise for me, and I didn't manage to talk to her.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: You had a sharp division of views, then -- sorry, Your Honour, I beg your pardon. You had a sharp division of views between the two members of the BiH Presidency, two Serb members, didn't you, Dr. Plavsic and Professor Koljevic?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I have to be honest. The fault lies with the three of us here. We should have explained this to Mrs. Plavsic, because when something is explained to her, she will at least remain silent, even if she doesn't agree. Obviously she was not kept abreast of matters and that is why she came out with her position and that caused disruption. So Mrs. Plavsic did not know what was going on, as opposed to the others, so I'm just saying what was realistic. It could have turned the Assembly in a completely different manner, in a different direction, because she was making a fiery speech and the MPs liked what she was saying. She was special. People like it when you're straightforward, when you're making a speech, but they don't realise at that time that it is an empty radicalism. Here I go with radicalism again. It's just an empty words, nice but empty.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: And then just to complete Mrs. Plavsic's contribution there, she says: "We are part of Yugoslavia, and only Yugoslavia can decide if she wants to enter into a relationship with the Muslim Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina, or the Croatian Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina, or any other such entity. "That is what is not clear to me." And then Dr. Karadzic starts off by saying: "Mrs. Plavsic is right," but then about four paragraphs further on, he says: "As to the mutual relations, we do not want to be accused of destroying Bosnia and Herzegovina. We are not opposed to Yugoslavia having links with them through us since we are in direct contact with them, since we are part of Yugoslavia ourselves. There is no reason why we should not have links with them if our relations are going to be based on equality. Since it is a complex constitutional arrangement, it will take time to be developed. But that does not in any way affect our right to remain within Yugoslavia and our right to keep our Yugoslav identity. "Therefore, if we have to preserve the Bosnian framework in one form or the other (everybody keeps saying that in some form Bosnia and Herzegovina must be preserved), okay, let's preserve some elements of Bosnia. Let some functions of the government remain shared." And then there is an interruption. "How are we going to pay for all that. We are already struggling to make ends meet!" Now, I can't be absolutely sure, Mr. Krajisnik, but that appears to be the first time that somebody has brought up starkly the question of money. Was that a -- was an intervention about, how we are going to pay for all that, was that something that you had anticipated?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know that you find this striking, but it is invariably important but money was not important here. All of these three peoples prefer a state. They like a state and their children equally. And all the rest is different. So this was just an excuse, who would pay for it and so on. There was just used by way of argument, but it was not the main argument for stating one's opposition.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Anyway, Dr. Karadzic completes his speech and he says: "Is my explanation clear enough?" And Dr. Plavsic: "Adds that it is too complicated and the idea that has emerged earlier today is much clearer." When she refers to "the idea that has emerged earlier today," is she -- is she harking back to preserving Bosnia and Herzegovina as simply as part of Yugoslavia, or is she talking about some other idea?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: When it says we gave a clearer picture, I believe that she means what she said. Her solution is much clearer than Mr. Karadzic's, who tried to wrap this nicely with different digressions, if I can put it that way. Quite simply, he was not in a position to say, "wait a minute, we have to give up on Yugoslavia now. We accept Bosnia and Herzegovina." Mrs. Plavsic says, "My situation is a clear-cut one. I want this and that." The idea was always there or, rather, not the idea but the position, that we want Bosnia in Yugoslavia, that we were not opposed to that. But what Mrs. Plavsic meant here was the Serb Bosnia and Herzegovina. That is to say, part of Serb Bosnia and Herzegovina. That is to say, that these two ethnic communities did not want that. That's what they showed. And if you said, well, we want them to go to Yugoslavia too, then that would mean imposing one's own will on them. Now, how -- that is what she doesn't say. Quite simply, two positions clashed. We are not going to impose our own will on others. We are not going to divide Bosnia, and then you see Mr. Karadzic saying, "We do not want to be accused of dividing Bosnia." Well, we can't. We kept saying that we were against the division of Bosnia. We want Bosnia to remain in Yugoslavia or to be transformed but not to divide it, because that was a forbidden be topic, forbidden under quotation marks, because somebody wanted to divide Bosnia, to cut a live tissue, if it can be put that way. So her position was clear. And then there were other people who took part in the debate and who spoke along similar lines. And so what she is saying is what we said is a clear position and what you are suggesting is not a clear position. That's Mr. Karadzic. But if you were to look at it formally that would be true. But the policy was that he wanted to familiarise them with the course that had to be taken because it came up as a necessity. The point was that we always wanted to reach agreement with the other two sides. That's our interest. We cannot do otherwise.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Then Dr. Kalinic speaks again in a way which -- well, doesn't give rise to questions immediately. And then you, Mr. Krajisnik --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Stewart, it seems that you're going to a new portion of the minutes. I'm looking at the clock.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: I'm entirely in Your Honour's hands. I would probably be another five minutes or so to get to the end of this document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let's then finish with this and take that five minutes. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: You, Mr. Krajisnik, then are the -- well, you're the last person to speak. You say -- I'll go to the second paragraph in what you say. "Everything must have its direction, its way of doing things, sequence of doing them. If you agree with me, and you already did so earlier, that decisions have been made today have to be seen through because we must not create any association that is against the interests of the Serbian people. Before we vote, I would urge you to bear in mind that you are sending a message to all of our citizens, to the Serbian people and others, that this Assembly has not made any decision that is aimed against honest Croats, Muslims, Yugoslavs or any other patriots. "The decision that we made today is aimed to save the state. That is our prerogative, that is our responsibility, and that is what we have done today. "Not a single decision of the Serbian Assembly has been aimed against any decision of the SDA or HDZ. Everything that we have done has been motivated by our desire to save our Serbian people, to save our constitutional order and the rule of law, to preserve our equality. "Therefore, I would urge you once again to send a clear message of what has been decided here today. Can you please vote about this piece of information, and this is a piece of information that is followed by other details which [would] be given in due course. "Do you agree with this piece of information?" And the Assembly unanimously support that. Mr. Krajisnik, where you say "not a single decision of the Serbian Assembly has been aimed against any decision of the SDA or the HDZ," was that -- was that 100 per cent correct?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Nothing in life is absolutely correct, but I'm almost sure, as far as I can tell, on the basis of my own thinking, that I never agreed or proposed that any decision be reached to the detriment of the other two peoples. I'm saying that not even gold is 100 per cent pure, but I'm convinced that this is so. We could not have done so. And that was not our interest either.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: As far as decisions were concerned, you were still left with the position where it appeared that the other -- the parties representing the other nations wanted independence of Bosnia and Herzegovina but that was not your primary position in the SDS, was it?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm sorry, your question is not clear, really.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: I'll break it up then. It still remained absolutely clear that the SDA and the HDZ were likely to proceed towards wanting or demanding independence of Bosnia and Herzegovina, didn't it?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: And it was -- remained the SDS primary position that it was against that.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: The SDS did not accept an untransformed Bosnia-Herzegovina. That was the point. We did not accept a sovereign Bosnia-Herzegovina the way the Muslims and Croats envisaged it to be, and that is a unitary Bosnia-Herzegovina. There is a major difference between a unitary Bosnia-Herzegovina on the one hand and, on the other hand, a transformed, decentralised state.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, would that be a convenient moment?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Stewart. We will adjourn until five minutes past 11.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Stewart, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Your Honours, the next matter I'm going to refer to is a document which has already been exhibited. We prepared some copies, Your Honour, because it's a relatively short document and it's relatively short notice. It's in P64A. That's Mr. Treanor. Tab 144, which is in binder 5. Your Honour, we've copied a version of the original B/C/S for Mr. Krajisnik if that could be got to him one way or another. And, Your Honour, it's a handwritten minutes of the SDS Deputies' Club meeting, 18th of October 1991. And, Your Honour, so it's described.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Mr. Krajisnik, you have that document, minutes of the session of the Club of Deputies of the SDS, Serbian Democratic Party of BH, held at 1630 on 18th of October, 1991, in the blue hall of the Assembly of BH. The session was attended by 49 deputies, and so on.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I see that.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Mr. Krajisnik, do you -- if you need to cast your eye down the page to answer that, can you say whether you were at that meeting?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe I was. I mean, I'm certain I was. I don't believe I wasn't. There may even be a contribution of mine somewhere below.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: One of the reasons I asked, Mr. Krajisnik, is that it doesn't appear that there is. That's all. It was -- but it was possible that you were there but never -- are not recorded as having made any specific contribution yourself. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have to say that I don't see from this that I actually said something.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Krajisnik, you've really answered that anyway. I want you to go to -- I've marked -- I've taken the liberty of marking in the margin just with a line, it's point 29 in the English. It's on page 4 of the English, and it's towards the end of the document you've got, Mr. Krajisnik.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Stewart, may I just interrupt you for one second? You say Mr. Krajisnik does not appear as one of the speakers. How should I understand almost at the bottom of the first page, is that a reference to what he said elsewhere or ...

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Well, actually, Your Honour, perhaps I was wrong. That is how I had understood it as a mention by somebody else of Mr. Krajisnik. But, Your Honour, perhaps I'm wrong about that. We better clarify it.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Mr. Krajisnik, do you see -- it may not be on the first page of yours but it's quite early in this document, there is a number 1 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It's the third page, approximately eight lines from the top in B/C/S, Mr. Krajisnik.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: "Debate and voting on the illegal resumption of the Assembly session on 14th October, 1991." Do you see that, Mr. Krajisnik?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: In Serbian, you said third page?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, the -- I have the first -- the page -- last three digits, ERN 500, after six lines it reads: "1," and then three lines down, I see "14th of October, 1991." And then it seems that it's your name first appearing on the fourth line under number 1.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, yes. That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Just to clarify, Mr. Krajisnik, whether that is in fact recording you talking or whether it's somebody else saying that you had done something.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: It says: "Krajisnik, colon" so that's supposed to be something I said. But actually these are notes made by the recording secretary who describes what I said, Krajisnik colon, et cetera. But I actually believe that's exactly what I said, the very words I used after that illegal session on the 14th.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Is it, Mr. Krajisnik, you think you were at this meeting?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think so, although I'm not quite sure. I have to be perfectly honest. There were many sessions. Maybe I attended some other session with another club. It was all at the Assembly. To be quite honest, I cannot say with absolute certainty but I think I think I was there.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: I think Your Honours will probably agree, we've carried that particular point as far as we can, Mr. Krajisnik. If you then go towards the end of this document, it's point 29. I have just marked it with a simple line in the margin on the left-hand side. It's on page -- the page that ends 506. You've got the numbering in top right-hand corner. It's the one that ends 506. Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I found it.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Dr. Karadzic is noted as speaking. He says: "A team made up of the leading men of the party, the government and the political council has been working day and night. I have decided to impose a state of emergency in the party. Please inform others that the party is working in emergency conditions. We must not make a single wrong step and we must listen to our leaders. Maximum discipline is required." Mr. Krajisnik, first of all, with that reference to "a team made up of the leading men of the party, the government and political council has been working day and night," were you one of any such team that had been working in the way he describes?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Maybe it's a good idea for me to explain the context in which Mr. Karadzic said this and then answer your question. I think that would be of greater assistance to you. Although if you prefer it that way, I can answer your question immediately but it won't be absolutely clear then.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Mr. Krajisnik, I feel there is no objection to your answering with the context first.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said already that I had already analysed this -- these minutes even before, so I have a very good idea of what these words of Mr. Karadzic's mean. Mr. Dragan Djokanovic was the previous speaker and he appeared as a witness here. And he mentions the war in a frenzied voice filled with panic. He says they had voted for independence, we were about to go to war. It was a very unpleasant discussion. And now, Mr. Karadzic is talking in response to the previous contribution. He is saying, "We are working, we have everything under control. There is a whole team of people working on it," to dissipate the tensions that arise when somebody says, "We should have gone to war already." And now to answer your question, there existed certain bodies, such as the party council, the ministerial council, there were commissions, there were experts, civil servants and the Executive Board of the SDS party. And just after the 14th and the 15th, the MPs were in favour of making some sort of radical move, and Karadzic is telling them, "Take it easy. We have a whole team working on it. We have things under control." That's a political message. All these people are working on it. And I have to be honest, in the ranks of the Serbs, in various circles, there was a lot of concern. We all debated and debated, but it was difficult to find a solution. It's easy to burn all the bridges but it's difficult to find a solution. You will see that all sorts of proposals had been made to that effect, so Mr. Karadzic was trying to play things down, to appease those present. This team was not just five or six men. All of us were debating this very difficult watershed that the Serbian people were facing. I hope I have answered your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Had a decision to impose a state of emergency in the party been taken by Dr. Karadzic in advance of this meeting of the Deputies' Club?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's difficult for me to say that, but I have to because I'm under oath. Mr. Karadzic kept saying all the time, "I'll impose a state of emergency. I'll tighten the discipline, tighten the screws." Maybe he indeed sent that kind of telegram but I assure you that everybody on the ground did not take that with particular concern. They were not particularly upset. We have, for instance, a place around Travnik, Zivinica where they would reply. We organised something in response, et cetera. So maybe you will find a piece of writing where Karadzic says, "We are hereby introducing a state of emergency," but this is a message aimed at people like Mr. Djokanovic who were saying, "We should go to war now." I don't think Mr. Djokanovic actually meant it, but for the audience who was hearing him, that could have caused fear and confusion. So Karadzic was saying, "We have to restore constitutionality. It's easy to make radical moves but let's do something constructive." So we were giving -- sending a political message to the other side, to return to the constitutional order, and then we'll deal with the rest easily. So we were saying, "You have a deadline until the 14th to return to the constitutional procedure and the constitutional order. And then we'll go back to the table."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: First of all, I'd like to ask you to slow down a bit. The interpreters are approximately three lines behind. And Judge Hanoteau would have a question for you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HANOTEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. Krajisnik, please, when we read what Mr. Djokanovic is saying, "[In English] I think we should go to war right away," [Interpretation] does this mean that many people in the SDS shared that opinion? Was that an opinion that only he had, or was there a group of SDS MPs who wanted to go to war right away?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, this is pure nonsense. Not a single serious person in the SDS thought this way. But this man was seized by panic when he said that. I know him. He's prone to panic. Nobody in the SDS wanted war. And my impression is nobody in the other parties wanted war either, especially not at this moment. So this is an isolated moment. That's why Mr. Karadzic reacted in this way, in order to alleviate the tensions, because somebody was bringing up the issue of war in December 1991, and we knew what was going on in Croatia and how dangerous it was to advocate something like that. He was in a different party, the party of federalists, but he attended this gathering because it was some sort of party gathering.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HANOTEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. But yesterday and today you told us about people who were more radical than others. So these people who were more radical than others, were they envisaging a war, a conflict. Yes. There was a conflict, after all, in the end.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, not in Bosnia. There was a conflict in Croatia.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HANOTEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. But later on, there was a war.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HANOTEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So at that moment, right now, when -- in October 1991, did you feel that among members of the SDS, there were people who were already ready to go to war, you know, and live through a war?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I absolutely can't remember a single member of the SDS whom I would have heard saying, "I think now is the moment we should go to war." Maybe there were individual radical statements, but it was out of the question that there was any desire to start a war. I didn't even hear it from the other side, apart from some people who were out of control. It would be wrong of me to say that the other side was advocating war. That's not true. I don't know why this man said what he said. That's the way I see it, at least.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HANOTEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And thank you. I tried to speak more slowly, and I always criticise those who speak fast, but I find it difficult to control myself at this moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Stewart will give you the good example, Mr. Krajisnik.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. I'll do my best.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Oh, Mr. Stewart speaks much faster than I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Mr. Krajisnik, taking it slowly, could we go up to point 6, back to point 6 in this same document? The numbered points -- this is probably a couple of pages into your copy.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: 501 for you, Mr. Krajisnik.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. It's points 5 and 6, and it's Mr. Radic speaking; do you see that? T. Radic? Do you see him?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. It's Trifko Radic, a MP from Ilijas. He was actually deputy president of the MPs' club.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: And he says: "I don't want to concern myself with this infamous Assembly anymore," he's obviously talking about the Bosnia-Herzegovina Assembly, "because we've already said everything. That's why we have to start working on a plebiscite of the Serbian people as soon as possible. "Will we continue to work in the Assembly? And can we work as the Serbian Assembly? What is the impact of the decision in The Hague on the Serbian people in BH? "My municipality, Ilijas, will disassociate itself from Sarajevo and join the Serb Autonomous District of Romanija. I kindly request the leadership to" -- well, that's not very clear. "We are preparing for war and the people want" -- Mr. Krajisnik we get in the translation, as written. Is it where it says "I kindly request the leadership to" -- is there something then in Serbian that you're able to read, the rest of that sentence? Read out to us, I mean, so that we can see what it says?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'll read it all so you have context. He says: "My municipality, Ilijas, will separate from Sarajevo and annex to SAO Romanija. I kindly request the leadership to" -- and then goes the next sentence -- "we are getting ready for war and people want" -- and then another incomplete sentence.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Yes, I see.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, the English translation is simply confirming that there is nothing there after those words.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: And then point 6: "We have to see what we ought to do. They are preparing for war - is that not clear?" Mr. Krajisnik, are you able to say whether that's Mr. Radic continuing speaking or whether it could be somebody else?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Let me just read it, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Yes, I'll read that whole paragraph 6 because it's the one I want to ask about anyway. "We have to see what we ought to do. They are preparing for war - is that not clear? You have our unqualified support for everything you're doing. The concentration of Croatian forces in the Neretva River valley is increasing daily. We are ready for war, and we can only defend Serbian honour with the rifle." Well, first of all, can you say who was speaking at that point?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: We don't see who is speaking here. But since there is a reference to the Neretva River valley, it cannot be Mr. Radic. It must be a MP from Herzegovina, because it's there that there was a concentration of Croatian forces, and the Neretva River valley is the area where Mostar is, the eastern and western Herzegovina. I can only guess who it was but I wouldn't be sure. Because one of the MPs repeatedly talked about the Neretva River valley.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: So when whichever MP that was was saying, "We are ready for war," what war or prospective war was he talking about?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: At this point, he's referring to -- it's pure marketing, actually, but he's saying we are ready to defend the Serb people in the Neretva River valley, to defend Serb honour. He's saying we are ready for war. I think it was a situation tainted by panic and everybody is talking from their own position. I think maybe the Yugoslav People's Army was still there. I can't say for sure. But "ready for war" does not mean that somebody actually wants war, but that they were mentally prepared to defend their area, defend Serbian honour. That's a bit poetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Mr. Krajisnik, perhaps I should make clear the clarification I'm seeking is this: We know, don't we, that the Croatian war had been going on for some considerable time by this point, hadn't it?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: And this MP refers to concentration of Croatian forces in the Neretva valley. But you agree his reference to "they are preparing for war," in saying "they are preparing for war," is he referring there to Muslims or Croats?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's in the first part of item 6, "They are preparing for war," he means the Croatian side. Let me say western Herzegovina, the border between eastern and western Herzegovina, and he means them.
